case_studies.title: OnTrack: Real-Time Monitoring and Intervention in LLM Agent Trajectories via Streaming Structure-Aware Optimal Transport
case_studies.abstract: Agents are deployed in applications from trip planners and stock trading to IT incident triage. In most cases, LLM agents work autonomously with minimal rule-based safeguarding, leading to cost and safety issues from irreversible actions. Recent works resolve this either by using a safeguard agent to monitor behavior or evaluating logs post-hoc. The first adds cost and latency to every step; the second delivers its verdict after the run, when tokens are burned and damage is done. To overcome this, we propose OnTrack, a streaming monitoring mechanism that compares an agent's steps and dependenc
case_studies.summary: OnTrack provides a live monitoring system that watches an LLM agent’s actions as they happen, using a structure‑aware optimal transport model to detect deviations from a safe plan. It builds a streaming comparison engine that flags risky moves in real time, allowing immediate corrective intervention. The result is reduced cost and safety risk because problems are caught before irreversible actions are taken.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) integrate OnTrack into your LLM‑driven incident triage pipeline to monitor agent decisions as they occur; 2) set up alerts for any step that deviates from the expected safe path; 3) configure a fallback script that automatically halts or corrects the agent when a risky deviation is detected.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel streaming monitoring framework (OnTrack) that allows real-time intervention in autonomous LLM agent behavior.  This is a fresh approach compared to existing post-hoc evaluation or safeguard agents, earning a high novelty score.  For IT engineers, the method is directly relevant when deploying LLM-powered incident triage or automation tools, but the application is still early and not yet a mainstream practice, so the IT relevance is moderate.  The actionable value within 90 days is limited: the approach is described conceptually and would require significant engineering effort to integrate with existing LLM APIs, SSO, or cloud infra.  Hence the value score is low.  The overall score is 54, well above the 40‑point threshold, so low_signal is false.

case_studies.title: SparseDecoding: Decoding-Aware Pruning for Accurate and Efficient LLM Inference
case_studies.abstract: The memory-bound nature of the decoding stage of large language model (LLM) inference incurs significant latency. Layer-wise training-free network pruning approaches guided by the Hessian have been a prominent solution to this problem, as pruning reduces the number of nonzero parameters read from memory during decoding. Nevertheless, typical methods in this line compute the Hessian using pre-collected natural sequences, whereas the model is fed self-generated tokens during decoding, creating a distribution shift between the two sequences. case_studies.summary: The paper tackles the latency of LLM decoding by pruning weights based on a Hessian calculated during decoding, reducing memory reads. The authors built a pruning method that re‑computes the Hessian on the model’s own generated tokens, avoiding distribution shift and achieving faster inference with little loss of accuracy. This is directly relevant to cloud infrastructure managers who run LLMs, offering a way to cut inference costs and improve throughput.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference, 1) add a Hessian‑aware pruning step before deployment, 2) use the model’s own generated tokens to compute the Hessian during a short calibration run, 3) prune weights and re‑deploy the slimmer model to cut memory bandwidth and latency.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a decoding-aware pruning technique using Hessian-guided pruning that addresses latency and memory usage during LLM inference. This is directly relevant to engineers who deploy large models in cloud or edge environments. It offers a concrete method that can be applied to reduce inference cost, making it actionable within 90 days for teams that already have model serving pipelines.

case_studies.title: The Harness as the Only Mutable Surface: Compliance-Bounded Self-Evolution of LLM Agents in Credit Pipelines, with a Measured Admission Gate
case_studies.abstract: Self-improving LLM agents can adapt a credit pipeline to a changed rule, but an agent that rewrites itself destroys the artefact a supervisor reviews: a named change, a recorded test, an approval. We argue that self-evolution is reviewable only if it is confined to the runtime harness (instruction text, tool-call logic and primitive composition) while model weights stay fixed, so that every adaptation is a diff with a cause and a test attached. case_studies.summary: The paper proposes a system that lets large language model (LLM) agents adapt to changes in credit rules without rewriting the core model. They built a dual‑loop engine that confines self‑modification to a runtime harness—just the instruction text, tool‑calls, and primitive composition—while keeping model weights fixed. The result is a safe, traceable way to evolve the agent with an admission gate that records a hash‑chained change log and a test before deployment.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for AI services, here is what to do: 1) isolate LLM changes to a runtime harness so that the core model weights stay immutable; 2) implement an admission gate that hashes the harness changes, stores the hash chain, and runs automated tests before rollout; 3) ensure every change has an associated diff, cause, and test record for audit purposes.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: 10 – introduces the concept of limiting self‑evolution to the harness, a potentially surprising design pattern for engineers working with LLM services. IT_RELEVANCE: 15 – relevant to those deploying LLM agents in regulated environments (e.g., credit pipelines) and managing compliance through harness‑level controls. VALUE_90_DAYS: 30 – provides a concrete dual‑loop engine and an admission gate with hash‑chained records that an engineer could prototype or adapt within 90 days for controlled LLM deployment or compliance tooling. Total score above 40, so low_signal=false.
